Understanding Precious Metal Purity
How karat and fineness standards determine the value, liquidity, and authenticity of gold and silver investments worldwide.
When archaeologists analyzed ancient Egyptian gold artifacts from King Tutankhamun’s tomb, they discovered the gold maintained purity levels of 85-95% after more than 3,000 years. That durability is why purity matters: it determines not just an investment’s value, but its liquidity and long-term recognition.
Whether you’re buying gold or silver, purity defines what you actually own and what someone else will pay for it later.
Gold Purity: The Karat System
The word “karat” comes from the carob seed, which ancient merchants used as a standard weight because of its remarkable consistency. Modern gold purity is expressed in karats (out of 24) or in fineness (parts per thousand).
24 Karat (999.9 fine):
99.99% pure gold — the standard for investment bullion
22 Karat (916.7 fine):
91.67% pure — used in coins like the American Gold Eagle and Krugerrand
18 Karat (750 fine):
75% pure — high-end jewelry and some collectible coins
14 Karat (583.3 fine):
58.33% pure — common in jewelry, not typically used for investment
10 Karat (416.7 fine):
41.67% pure — minimum legal standard for gold jewelry in the US
💡
Ancient Wisdom
The ancient Lydians (around 700 BC) were among the first to systematically test gold purity using touchstones — scratching gold on dark basaltic stone and applying acid to read the color reaction. Variants of the method are still used today.
Silver Purity: The Sterling Standard
Silver’s purity standards trace back to medieval England and still anchor global markets.
999.9 Fine Silver:
99.99% pure — investment-grade bars
999 Fine Silver:
99.9% pure — most bullion coins, including the American Silver Eagle and Canadian Maple Leaf
Sterling Silver (925):
92.5% pure — traditional jewelry and flatware
Coin Silver (900):
90% pure — US silver coins minted before 1965
German Silver (800):
80% pure — European jewelry and decorative arts
📊
Historical Trivia
The term “sterling silver” likely derives from the Norman French “esterlin,” referring to small silver coins. The 925 standard was codified in England by 1238 AD under King Henry III and has held for nearly 800 years.
Investment Grade vs. Jewelry Grade
Understanding the difference between investment-grade and jewelry-grade metals can meaningfully change your returns.
Investment-grade characteristics
Gold:
Minimum 995 fine (99.5% pure) for most investment products
Silver:
Minimum 999 fine (99.9% pure) for bullion
Global recognition:
Accepted by dealers worldwide without question
Easier liquidation:
No purity calculations needed at resale
Lower premiums:
Less manufacturing cost compared with jewelry
The economics of purity
Here is how purity actually affects value at resale:
A 1 oz 24K gold coin trades close to spot
A 1 oz 18K gold piece contains 75% of spot’s worth of gold by weight
But the selling price might be only 60-70% of that gold-content value once dealer margins and refining costs are deducted
That gap is why bullion buyers gravitate toward 999.9 bars and recognized sovereign coins rather than scrap jewelry.
→
Modern Testing
Modern XRF (X-ray fluorescence) machines determine metal content to roughly 0.01% accuracy in seconds — without damaging the piece. It’s a long way from the touchstone, but the underlying question is the same: is this really what it claims to be?
Hallmarks and Stamps
Every piece of precious metal tells its story through small stamps that reveal purity, origin, and authenticity.
Common gold hallmarks
“999.9” or “9999”:
24 karat fine gold
“916” or “22K”:
22 karat gold
“750” or “18K”:
18 karat gold
“585” or “14K”:
14 karat gold
Common silver hallmarks
“999” or “.999”:
Fine silver bullion
“925” or “Sterling”:
Sterling silver
“900”:
Coin silver
Mint marks:
Indicate where the coin was produced
💡
Counterfeit Protection
Authentic hallmarks are difficult to fake well. The British hallmarking system began in 1238 AD, making it one of the world’s oldest forms of consumer protection — some London assay offices have operated continuously for over 700 years.
Testing Methods: Ancient to Modern
Understanding how purity is tested helps you verify holdings and avoid counterfeits.
Traditional methods
Touchstone testing:
Scratch test with acid — still used today
Fire assay:
Melting samples for precise destructive analysis
Specific gravity:
Weight-to-volume ratio testing
Magnet test:
Pure gold and silver are not magnetic
Modern technology
XRF analysis:
X-ray fluorescence for instant, non-destructive results
Electronic testing:
Conductivity-based purity detection
Ultrasonic testing:
Sound wave analysis for internal composition
Sigma Metalytics:
Electromagnetic testing that works through plastic packaging
⚠️
Buyer Tip
Buy from established dealers who provide assay or mint certificates and offer a published buyback policy. The hallmark and the institution behind it both matter.
Global Standards
Purity standards vary by region, but international acceptance comes down to meeting a few criteria.
Major global bodies
London Bullion Market Association (LBMA):
Sets global Good Delivery standards for gold and silver
COMEX:
New York commodities exchange standards for deliverable bars
Shanghai Gold Exchange (SGE):
Growing influence in Asian markets
ISO 9001:
International quality management framework
Regional preferences
North America:
Prefers 999.9 fine gold and silver bullion
Europe:
Accepts 995+ fine gold; strong hallmarking traditions
Asia:
999+ fine preferred, with growing demand for certified products
Middle East:
Traditional preference for 22K gold in both jewelry and investment
Matching Purity to Strategy
Your goals should guide your purity choices, because different purities serve different purposes.
For long-term wealth preservation
Choose maximum purity: 999.9 fine gold and silver
Focus on globally recognized products such as American Eagles, Canadian Maples, and Krugerrands
Avoid unusual alloys; stick to standard compositions for liquidity
For portfolio diversification
Mix purities deliberately — for example, a core of high-purity bullion with a smaller numismatic sleeve
Weigh premiums against purity; sometimes a slightly lower-purity sovereign coin carries a smaller spread than a generic bar
Diversify across mints and countries to spread sovereign and refiner risk
The Bottom Line
Purity is the technical backbone of every precious metals transaction. When you understand what those small stamps and fineness numbers mean, you stop buying “gold” or “silver” in the abstract and start buying a specific, verifiable claim on a specific quantity of metal.
That is what makes a bar or coin liquid anywhere in the world: not the brand, but the standard behind the hallmark. Choose investment-grade purity, buy from dealers who stand behind the assay, and the rest of the portfolio decisions get a lot easier.
